title: 75 to 16 days
text:
When deals drag on for months, look at how much you're asking for in the first conversation.

One client I worked with, a forest carbon scale-up, was asking landowners to commit their land for 50 years. They were often older and traditional, cynical about carbon credits, and thinking about their children. Sales were struggling, and deals took 75 days on average.

We changed four things;

1. Who we sold to. Professional owners who were ready to commit, not anyone with land.
2. How the team worked. We split it into SDRs and AEs, so booking meetings and closing deals were separate jobs.
3. What we said. Their problems and hurdles first, including the fear of being locked in for 50 years.
4. Who we spoke to. We mapped every stakeholder and brought them in early. Often that was the whole family.

In the end, these sales were all about trust.

The average sales cycle went from 75 days to 16. Deals got bigger too: in one market the average deal went from about €5–10k to around €70k at its peak. Quarterly sales went from about €0.1M to €5.4M in nine months (both estimated on the company's own model).

My takeaway: find the right things to change, and sell to the people who are ready to say yes.

What's the one change that would speed up your sales right now?

title: I put an AI version of my voice on my website
text:
I've put an AI version of my voice on my website.

It's interesting. It's also a bit creepy.

It's built on everything on my site: how I work, my case studies and how I fix sales. You can have a proper chat with it about what's stuck in your sales, and it'll point you to a next step. It tells you it's an AI straight away, and I read every conversation.

Why? I'm testing loads of new AI tools at the moment, and the best way to understand them is to build with them. And speed matters in sales. At one company I worked with, we got first replies to inbound leads from about a day to five minutes, with AI agents.

title: The 95% rule
text:
Many sales teams are struggling to make AI work.

I think a big reason is trust. They switch the agent on, then find out what it said to their best prospects.

You already have most of what you need to fix that: your past deals, your emails, and what your best people actually sent. Test on your own data first, and get to a confidence level before anything goes out.

This is how I do it, and how I've done it;

1. Shadow. The agent drafts for every lead, and nobody sees it. Compare its drafts with what your team actually sent.
2. Approve. A person approves, edits or rejects every draft. Track one number: approved without edits.
3. Automate. Once a segment hits 95% approved without edits, over enough volume, it can send on its own.
4. Audit. Keep sampling. If quality slips, it goes back to approval.

The edits are the most valuable part. Each one becomes an example that makes the next draft better.

How are you deciding when an AI workflow is good enough to go live?

If you're building AI into your sales process and want to do it in a way you can trust, my approach is here: harryjamescoburn.com/ai

title: First reply in five minutes
text:
How long does a new inbound lead wait for your first reply?

At one company I worked with, the answer was about a day. That's a long wait for a buyer who's ready to talk.

So we built AI agents to do the first part of the job. Every inbound lead was researched, qualified and answered within minutes. The best ones went straight to an SDR.

First reply went from about a day to five minutes. The share of inbound leads that sales qualified went from about 25% to 40%.

One thing we didn't automate: judgement. A person still approved every message before it went out, until we trusted what the agents sent.

Speed wins the first conversation. Trust wins the deal.

How fast does your team reply to a new lead today?

title: Hold the price
text:
When a buyer pushes on price, most sales teams reach for a discount.

I'd push back with value instead.

You set your price for a reason. If you drop it the moment someone asks, you're telling the buyer it was never worth that in the first place.

So when the price question comes:

1. Go back to the problem. What does it cost them if nothing changes?
2. Show the return. What do they get back, and how fast?
3. Hold the number with confidence. If something has to give, change the scope.

And if you're always in a price war, look at who you're selling to. Price wars usually mean the wrong customer.

A product treated as valuable earns more respect.

When did you last hold your price and win the deal anyway?

title: When Covid hit
text:
When the market drops overnight, the instinct is to go quiet and wait.

When Covid hit in 2020, I was leading B2B sales at a premium chauffeur company. Business travel stopped almost overnight.

So we called every client and listened. Safety came up again and again.

So we made safety the reason to choose us.

From the low, B2B revenue grew 912% between April and December 2020.

The lesson I took from it: when things go wrong, get closer to your customers, not further away. They'll tell you what matters now.

When did your customers last tell you something that changed how you sell?

If your sales have stalled, my 2-minute scorecard shows you where to start: harryjamescoburn.com/scorecard

title: Be clear who you're for
text:
If selling feels hard, look at who you're selling to before you look at how.

Most teams I meet are chasing anyone who'll take a meeting. Lots of activity, lots of small deals, a pipeline nobody trusts.

I'd rather close a few of the right customers than many of the wrong ones.

Here's the test I use:

1. Pull your last 20 wins and losses.
2. Write down what your best customers have in common.
3. Stop chasing the ones that look nothing like them.

When you get this right, the message gets sharper, deals move faster and price stops being the fight.

Be clear who you're for, and selling gets easy.

Who's the customer you should stop chasing?

title: Fix the bucket first
text:
Many CEOs want AI in their sales process before they know where their revenue leaks.

Picture your funnel as a bucket. Leads in the top, revenue out the bottom, and holes on the way down.

Pour AI into a leaky bucket and you get more water on the floor, faster.

Before you automate anything, ask four questions:

1. Customer: who actually buys, and who just takes meetings?
2. Message: can everyone on the team say who you're for in one sentence?
3. Flow: where do most deals stall?
4. Price: are you selling on value, or discounting to close?

Fix the biggest hole first. Then let AI speed up the work around it.

Where does your bucket leak most?

This week's newsletter goes deeper, with what it looked like at one company: harryjamescoburn.substack.com

title: Every stalled deal
text:
When a market stalls, more pipeline is usually not the answer.

At one company, our UK sales had stalled. There were deals in the pipeline, but they weren't closing.

So I worked every stalled UK deal myself, one by one, until it signed.

Then we sold bottom up. We found riders who were already expensing trips and took that evidence to their employer.

UK sales went up 75% in two months.

The deals you already have are often worth more than the ones you're chasing.

How many deals in your pipeline have been stuck for more than a month?

title: Will AI take the first sales call?
text:
Some people think AI voice agents will soon take over SDR qualification calls. I'm genuinely not sure.

I've put an AI version of my own voice on my website, so I can see why people think it. It can hold a real conversation, ask good questions and book the next step. It's impressive, and a little strange.

The case for: every lead gets a call within minutes, day or night, and SDRs spend their time on the conversations that need a person.

The case against: qualification is often the first moment a buyer decides whether to trust you. I believe the moments that matter should stay with people.

The world is changing fast, and I don't think anyone has this fully figured out yet.

So I'd like to hear from you. Would you take a qualification call from an AI if it told you it was one? And would you put one in front of your own buyers?

Try mine and tell me what you think: harryjamescoburn.com/ai

title: Two kinds of work
text:
Many teams are rolling AI out across the whole sales process, including the moments where a buyer decides whether to trust them.

I split sales into two kinds of work.

The work around the moments: research, routing, CRM updates, first drafts, call notes. Automate as much of it as you can.

The moments that matter: qualification, the demo, the stakeholder questions, the negotiation. Keep a person there, and use AI to make them better prepared.

Give AI the admin. Keep the trust.

Which step in your sales process would you never hand to AI?

This week's newsletter has the full list, and how to sort yours: harryjamescoburn.substack.com

title: Ask why five times
text:
When a buyer tells you their problem, they're usually telling you the first layer.

"We need more leads." Why? "Pipeline is down." Why? "Our best reps left." Why?

Keep going. I ask why at least five times before I pitch anything.

The fifth answer is usually the real problem, and it's rarely the one they opened with.

Then give your champion something they can use: the problem in their words, what it's costing them, and what changes if they fix it. They're the one who has to sell it inside the company when you're not in the room.

What's the first answer your buyers give you that you've learned not to believe?

title: Process scales, talent doesn't
text:
Every CEO wants to hire a star salesperson. I understand why. But it's a risky way to build a sales team.

Stars leave. They have bad quarters. And what they know usually lives in their head.

I believe a strong process beats exceptional individuals. Get the system right and anyone on the team can execute it, and AI can scale it.

That means writing down what your best people do: who they talk to, what they ask, what they send, and when they walk away. Then teaching it to everyone else.

Process can scale. Talent can't.

If your best seller left tomorrow, what would walk out the door with them?

If you want to see how strong your system is, my 2-minute scorecard is here: harryjamescoburn.com/scorecard

title: The bar is higher for outbound
text:
Many teams are using AI to send more outbound, faster. That's where I'd be most careful.

Inbound buyers asked to hear from you. Outbound buyers didn't.

So before any AI writes outbound for you, it needs the highest confidence: the right person, at the right time, in the right context. Personalisation that's wrong is worse than none.

My rule: no AI workflow sends on its own until it sends what we would send, at least 95% of the time. For outbound, I'd hold that bar the longest.

How do you check what your AI outbound actually says?
